headline: Hearts Can Heal Themselves After Attack, Scientists Find
meta_description: Researchers at University of Sydney prove human hearts can regrow muscle cells after heart attack, challenging decades of medical assumptions.
summary_short: For the first time, scientists have shown that human heart muscle can regenerate after a heart attack—a discovery that could transform how we treat heart failure.
body:
For decades, doctors have accepted a grim reality: when a heart attack destroys heart muscle, that damage is permanent. Researchers from the University of Sydney, the Baird Institute, and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital have now overturned this assumption. They've demonstrated that the human heart can produce new muscle cells after an attack—the first time this regenerative capacity has been proven in humans. While the heart remains scarred, and the natural regrowth isn't currently strong enough to reverse all damage, the finding opens a path toward therapies that could amplify this self-repair process and potentially prevent heart failure. "Our research shows that while the heart is left scarred after a heart attack, it produces new muscle cells, which opens up new possibilities," explained Dr. Robert Hume, first author of the study published in Circulation Research.

The stakes are enormous. Cardiovascular disease kills nearly one quarter of all Australians and remains the leading cause of death worldwide. A single heart attack can destroy as many as one third of the heart's cells. While survival rates have improved, many patients later develop heart failure—a condition where the heart can no longer pump blood effectively. Australia has approximately 144,000 people living with heart failure, yet only about 115 heart transplants are performed annually, leaving a critical shortage of treatment options.

The breakthrough relied on an innovative approach: researchers collected tissue samples from living patients during heart bypass surgery at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital. Studying tissue from actual human hearts rather than animal models gives scientists far more reliable data about how the heart naturally attempts to heal. "Using living human heart tissue models in our work means that we will have more accurate and reliable data to develop new therapies," said Professor Sean Lal, senior author of the study. The research has already identified several proteins involved in heart regeneration—clues that could help scientists learn how to encourage damaged hearts to generate more muscle cells and eventually reverse heart failure.
quick_facts: First proof that human hearts regrow muscle cells after heart attack
Study from University of Sydney, Baird Institute, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital
144,000 Australians living with heart failure; only 115 transplants yearly
Heart attack can destroy up to one third of heart cells
Researchers used tissue from living patients during bypass surgery
